content:
A short argument has been circulating on social media. The Quran calls God "the First and the Last" (57:3). In the Book of Revelation, Jesus says, "I am the first and the last" (Revelation 1:17).

So, the argument runs, the Quran confirmed Revelation, and Muhammad (peace be upon him) indirectly affirmed that Jesus is God. Jesus, it adds, is the true face of al-Rahman al-Rahim, the Most Merciful, the Most Compassionate.

The argument deserves a careful answer, because it rests on a real overlap: the same title does appear in both books. This article aims to provide context to the argument, insha'Allah, in seven answers: what the title means in the Quran, what it means in Revelation, whether a shared title makes a shared identity, and what the Quran itself says about Jesus and about the name al-Rahman.

Revelation uses the title three times. "Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one" (1:17). "The words of the first and the last, who died and came to life" (2:8).

"I am the Alpha and the Omega, the first and the last, the beginning and the end" (22:13). In the first two the speaker is plainly the risen Jesus. The title comes from Isaiah, where God says, "I am the first and I am the last; besides me there is no god" (Isaiah 44:6; compare 41:4 and 48:12).[1]

A fair account should grant what is true in the argument. The author of Revelation chose Isaiah's title on purpose, and the New Testament scholar Richard Bauckham has argued at length that he meant to include Jesus in the identity of the God of Israel.

Revelation honours Jesus with the title. The question is whether the Quran's use of the same words confirms that reading, and whether Revelation itself, read as a whole, supports it.[1]

The argument assumes that when two books use the same title, they mean the same thing by it. The Quran shows why that does not follow. It calls the Prophet "kind and merciful" (ra'uf rahim, 9:128), using two words that are also names of God (2:143).

It tells him to say, "I have been commanded to be the first of those who submit" (6:14; compare 39:12). No Muslim has ever concluded from these verses that Muhammad is God, or that he is "the First" in God's sense.

The meaning is decided by what the text says about the one who bears the word. The Bible works the same way. God says to the judges of Israel, "You are gods, sons of the Most High, all of you; nevertheless, like men you shall die" (Psalm 82:6-7), and Jesus quotes the verse in John 10:34.

No reader takes it to make the judges divine. So the right question is: what does each book say about its "First and Last"?[2]

The verse reads in full: "He is the First and the Last, the Outward and the Inward, and He has knowledge of all things" (57:3). The Prophet explained it in a prayer he taught for bedtime: "O God, You are the First, and there is nothing before You; You are the Last, and there is nothing after You; You are the Outward, and there is nothing above You; You are the Inward, and there is nothing beyond You."[3]

Al-Tabari, the great commentator of the tenth century, explains the two names in the same terms: God is "the First, before everything, without limit, and the Last, after everything, without end. That is said because He was when nothing existed besides Him, and He will be after all things have perished, as He said: 'Everything perishes except His Face' (28:88)." The Quran's First and Last is the one who outlasts all death. Elsewhere it calls Him "the Living who does not die" (25:58).[4]

Now read Revelation 1:17 to the end of the sentence. "Fear not, I am the first and the last, and the living one. I died, and behold I am alive forevermore, and I have the keys of Death and Hades" (1:17-18). The letter to Smyrna says the same: "the first and the last, who died and came to life" (2:8).

On the Quran's meaning, the one who is the Last is the one after whom nothing remains and who does not die. A First and Last who died, however briefly, is not the First and Last of 57:3. Far from confirming Revelation 1:17, the Quran's verse sets a standard that the speaker in Revelation 1:18 does not meet by his own account.

Christian theologians answer that Jesus died in his human nature, not his divine nature. That answer has a long history, and our article Can God die? weighs it. But it concedes the point at issue here: the divine nature, the true First and Last, did not die, and the one who said "I died" was speaking as a man.[5]

Revelation does give Jesus very high honour. In one vision every creature praises "him who sits on the throne and the Lamb" together (5:13).

A fair reader should say so. But the same book draws a line between Jesus and God from its first verse to its last.

The book opens: "The revelation of Jesus Christ, which God gave him" (1:1). God gives, and Jesus receives. Jesus has made believers "priests to his God and Father" (1:6).

In the letters to the churches the risen Jesus speaks of "my God" five times: "I have not found your works complete in the sight of my God" (3:2), and four times in one verse, "the temple of my God... the name of my God, and the name of the city of my God... which comes down from my God out of heaven" (3:12). He calls himself "the beginning of God's creation" (3:14). In the throne-room vision the Lamb comes and takes the scroll "from the right hand of him who was seated on the throne" (5:7).[6]

The one who says "my God" is not the God he speaks of. Revelation's Jesus has a God, and in Islam, God has no God.

Jesus says the same in the Gospels: "I am ascending to my Father and your Father, to my God and your God" (John 20:17). Our article Did Jesus pray, and to whom? follows the theme through the Gospels.

The argument says the Quran "affirmed" Revelation. The Quran describes its relation to earlier scripture in a single verse: "We have sent down to you the Book in truth, confirming what was before it of the Scripture and as a guardian over it" (5:48).

The word for guardian, muhaymin, means a witness and judge. Where the earlier books agree with it, the Quran confirms them; where later belief has drifted, the Quran corrects it.[7]

On the question of Jesus the Quran speaks plainly, in verses of its own. "They have disbelieved who say that God is the Messiah, son of Mary, while the Messiah said, 'O Children of Israel, worship God, my Lord and your Lord'" (5:72). "The Messiah, son of Mary, was only a messenger... They both used to eat food" (5:75).

In the scene of judgement Jesus himself denies the claim: "I said to them nothing except what You commanded me: worship God, my Lord and your Lord" (5:117). A reader who wants to know what Muhammad affirmed about Jesus has these verses. They leave no room for the inference.[7]

A note on history belongs here too. Revelation was written, by the early report of Irenaeus, toward the end of the reign of Domitian, about 95. Its place in the canon was disputed for centuries.

Dionysius of Alexandria in the third century doubted that it was written by the apostle John, Eusebius listed it both among the accepted books and among the disputed ones, Cyril of Jerusalem left it out of his list of scripture, and the Syriac Peshitta did not include it. The churches of the East were slow to read in their services the very book on which this argument rests.[8]

The argument ends with the claim that Jesus shows "true al-Rahman al-Rahim." The Quran answers this almost word for word, and with the very name: "They say, 'Al-Rahman has taken a son.' You have done an atrocious thing. The heavens almost rupture from it, and the earth splits open, and the mountains collapse in devastation, that they attribute to al-Rahman a son. And it is not fitting for al-Rahman that He should take a son. There is no one in the heavens and the earth but that he comes to al-Rahman as a servant" (19:88-93).[9]

The classical scholars noticed something about the two names. Al-Baghawi writes that creatures may be called rahim, merciful, but "none other than God is called Rahman." Al-Tabari observes that some creatures are called one or the other, but that the two together, rahman rahim, "have never been joined for anyone but Him, and are not joined for anyone else." The Prophet can be rahim (9:128).

Jesus can be "a mercy from Us" (19:21). Neither is al-Rahman.[10]

The Quran gives Jesus his own words in the cradle: "Indeed, I am the servant of God. He has given me the Scripture and made me a prophet" (19:30). And it adds: "Never would the Messiah disdain to be a servant of God" (4:172). In al-Faruqi's statement of tawhid, Creator and creature are two orders of being, and "it is forever impossible that the one be united with, infused, confused with or diffused into the other." A servant of al-Rahman, however honoured, stays on the servant's side of that line.[9][11]

The bottom line

The Quran and Revelation share the words "the First and the Last," and both take them from Isaiah, where they belong to the God beside whom there is no other. In the Quran, the Prophet's own prayer and the classical commentators explain the title: nothing before Him, nothing after Him, and He does not die. In Revelation, the one who uses the title says "I died," says "my God," and receives his revelation from God.

A shared phrase does not make a shared belief. The Quran guards the earlier scripture by judging it, and on Jesus its judgement is explicit: a messenger and a servant of al-Rahman, who told his people to worship "God, my Lord and your Lord." God knows best.

Notes

  1. Revelation 1:17; 2:8; 22:13; Isaiah 41:4; 44:6; 48:12. Bible quotations follow the English Standard Version. Richard Bauckham, The Theology of the Book of Revelation (Cambridge: Cambridge University Press, 1993), chapter 3.
  2. Quran 9:128; 2:143; 6:14; 39:12; Psalm 82:6–7; John 10:34.
  3. Quran 57:3. Sahih Muslim 2713, report of Abu Hurayra.
  4. Al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan (Mecca: Dar al-Tarbiya wa-l-Turath, n.d.; vols. 1–16 ed. Mahmud Muhammad Shakir), vol. 23, p. 168, on Quran 57:3, https://shamela.ws/book/43/13404; Quran 28:88; 25:58.
  5. Revelation 1:17–18; 2:8.
  6. Revelation 1:1; 1:6; 3:2; 3:12; 3:14; 5:7; 5:13; John 20:17.
  7. Quran 5:48; 5:72; 5:75; 5:116–117.
  8. Irenaeus, Against Heresies 5.30.3; Eusebius, Ecclesiastical History 3.25 and 7.25; Cyril of Jerusalem, Catechetical Lectures 4.36; Bruce M. Metzger, The Canon of the New Testament (Oxford: Clarendon Press, 1987), on the reception of Revelation in the East.
  9. Quran 19:88–93; 19:30; 4:172.
  10. Al-Baghawi, Ma'alim al-Tanzil, and al-Tabari, Jami al-Bayan, vol. 1, pp. 114–134, on Quran 1:1, https://shamela.ws/book/43/126; Quran 9:128; 19:21.
  11. Ismail Raji al-Faruqi, Al Tawhid: Its Implications for Thought and Life, 2nd edition (Herndon: International Institute of Islamic Thought, 1992), chapter 1.
